text: dsh-power-switch 是面向 Windows 的 DSH 插件，在侧边栏提供关闭按钮，并在设置的插件页提供电源卡片。用户可确认后关闭 DSH，也可选择下次以普通标签页或应用窗口启动；切换时插件会保存模式、处理桌面快捷方式并重启 DSH。卡片还提供退出等待、退出码和强制退出等高级设置。适合希望直接从 DSH 界面管理本机进程和启动窗口方式的 Windows 用户；需要 Windows、Node.js 20 及兼容版本的 DSH，不需要 API 密钥或外部账号。

dsh-power-switch adds Windows DSH controls to shut down the process and choose whether the next launch opens in a tab or app window. Its sidebar and Plugins card save the choice, update the desktop shortcut, and restart DSH. Requires Windows, Node.js 20, and compatible DSH; no API key is needed.

A DeepSeek Harness (DSH) plugin providing two features:

dsh-power-switch README · dsh-power-switch：- **Process shutdown**: a `⏻` button in the sidebar foot (with confirmation) that shuts down the local `dsh web` process through DSH's own graceful exit path, so sessions and settings are flushed first.
- **Launch mode switch**: a switch on the Settings -> Plugins card that selects how the next launch opens — an app window or a normal tab. A single press saves the setting, updates the desktop shortcut and restarts DSH.
dsh-power-switch README · Platform support：Windows only. `package.json` declares `"os": ["win32"]`, so other platforms cannot install it.

dsh-power-switch README · Platform support：App-window mode depends on a desktop shortcut (Windows Script Host and `.lnk`), for which there is no equivalent yet. The shutdown feature itself is platform-independent (it goes through `ctx.appExit` and never calls a shell), but shipping a plugin whose primary feature would silently degrade on macOS/Linux is worse than declaring no support. Adding it later requires `open`/`xdg-open`, macOS browser paths and a `.desktop` equivalent.

dsh-power-switch README · Requirements：The DSH range is spelled per minor line, and that is not decoration: DSH has only ever published prereleases, and semver admits a prerelease into a range only when a comparator **on the same `major.minor.patch`** carries a prerelease of its own — so `*`, `>=0.1.0` and a bare `>=0.1.6-alpha.2` all admit no DSH build that exists. The floor is the first DSH release shipping `@deepseek-ai/dsh-plugin-manager`: before it there is no `dsh plugin install` and no `dsh.bundle` layer, so this package cannot be installed at all. Tested against `0.1.6-alpha.2` (the full suite), the `0.1.7` line and `0.2.0-rc.2` (the desktop app); a new DSH minor line needs another branch here.

dsh-power-switch README · Requirements：The `0.2.0-*` branch was checked against the implementation rather than copied from a version string: in `0.2.0-rc.2` the `@deepseek-ai/dsh-host-webserver` package still exposes the `webServer` service on `extends Service`, and the `register({ kind, path, handler })` signature, the duplicate-route throw, the returned disposer and the `port` getter are all unchanged. Its own `@deepseek-ai/schemastery` dependency (`~3.18.4`) also falls inside this package's `>=3.18.1 <4`.

dsh-power-switch README · Verifying and uninstalling：- Verify: the profile's `dsh.profile.bundles` contains this plugin, and `node_modules\dsh-power-switch` is an ordinary directory (a local `link:` install is a symbolic link or junction).
- Uninstall: `dsh plugin --profile web remove dsh-power-switch`. The desktop shortcut does not depend on the package, so nothing has to be undone first — but if the mode is app window, switch back to the normal tab in the card before removing it if you want your original launch method back immediately. Otherwise the next double-click of the icon does it: the copy the shortcut points at notices the package is gone, puts the original shortcut back, and says so. `restore-shortcut.vbs` in the state directory does the same thing by hand.
- Return to a local checkout: uninstall first, then run `dsh plugin --profile web add link:<absolute path to this checkout>`; both steps should carry the one-shot flag above.
- Do not install the GitHub build and a local `link:` build into the same profile: the package name is identical, so the later install replaces the earlier one.
dsh-power-switch README · Verifying and uninstalling：> `dsh plugin` writes into `$DSH_HOME/profiles/web/`. If dsh runs under a sandbox, run it from an ordinary terminal.

dsh-power-switch README · Shutdown：The sidebar `⏻`, the card's "Shut down DSH" button and the `POST /api/dsh-power-switch/shutdown` route behave identically. Both controls first show a confirmation dialog, and that dialog also offers **Restart** — see [Restart](#restart) for what it does:

dsh-power-switch README · Shutdown：1. The response is sent before the exit begins, so the page can report that shutdown was requested; no response within 10 seconds is reported as a failure.
2. The exit is graceful: sessions and settings are flushed, and the plugin tree is disposed.
3. If that disposal stalls, a watchdog forces the process to end when its deadline expires.

dsh-power-switch README · Shutdown：The `appExit` service becomes available progressively while the host boots. A shutdown triggered in the first moments, before that service is registered, falls back to `SIGTERM` (measured log line: `no appExit service; sending SIGTERM to self`). Where a graceful exit must be guaranteed, wait a few seconds after startup before shutting down.

dsh-power-switch README · Shutdown：In app-window mode the page closes itself once the process is gone. In normal-tab mode a browser refuses to let a page close a tab the user opened, so the card states to press **Ctrl+W**. That is a browser restriction, not a gap in the plugin.

dsh-power-switch README · Shutdown："The process is gone" is the moment the window closes, and that is what makes `delayMs` visible: with a 10 s wait the window stays up for about 10 s and then closes with the process it belongs to. Both power controls work this way. The sidebar button used to close the window as soon as the host **accepted** the request — a different moment, and one that looked broken as soon as the wait became real.

dsh-power-switch README · Restart：Restarting is the third option in the confirmation dialog both power controls open (Cancel / **Restart DSH** / Shut down), it is the last step of the mode switch, and it stands on its own when the launch about to be replaced is the only thing you want to change:

```powershell

dsh-power-switch README · double-click scripts\restart-dsh-web.vbs, or run the script directly：node scripts\restart-dsh-web.mjs --delay-seconds 3
```

The dialog option and the script use `POST /api/dsh-power-switch/restart`; the dialog sends **no mode**, so it restarts into whatever mode is already configured — it replaces the process and nothing else, and it never touches the desktop shortcut.

When that confirmation does not arrive the host keeps serving and the answer says why — a refusal is always better than a service that never comes back. What "the recorded launch command" means, and the refusals that apply, are described under [Launch mode](#launch-mode-app-window--normal-tab); the same rules govern this entry.

text:
dsh-power-switch README · Launch mode: app window / normal tab：| | App window | Normal tab |
|---|---|---|
| Opened as | Chromium `--app=` (no address bar or tab strip) | a tab in the default browser |
| Size | fills the work area of the screen it opens on | wherever the browser puts a tab |
| After a shutdown | the page closes itself | press Ctrl+W |
section: Launch mode: app window / normal tab

text: dsh-power-switch README · Launch mode: app window / normal tab：The window's size is set by the **page**, not by the launching command line, and that is measured rather than preferred. Once a Chromium browser already has an instance running — which it does whenever DSH is on screen — it hands the URL to that instance, which creates the window with its own bounds and never reads the switches of the command line that handed the URL over: a bare `--app=<url>` measured 1010x1084 on a 2048x1152 screen, and `--start-maximized`, `--window-size=1920,1080 --window-position=0,0`, `--kiosk` and `--start-fullscreen` all measured the same half-width window. What does work is the page moving and resizing its own app window (`resizeTo` took it from 1010x1085 to 1202x702 in the same measurement series).
section: Launch mode: app window / normal tab

text: dsh-power-switch README · Launch mode: app window / normal tab：That is why the launcher opens the window on the plugin's own page rather than on DSH: `/api/dsh-power-switch/app-window?next=<the authenticated URL>` fills the work area as its **first** action and then replaces itself with that URL. Opening DSH directly left the window at the browser's default size for as long as DSH's own boot took — the half-width window that then jumped. With the hand-over page the window is already filled when it appears: a watcher polling every 40 ms from before the launch saw exactly one size, `2048x1104 at 0,0`, with the hand-over already done. The page accepts only a loopback `http` URL carrying a token, because a browser follows its redirect, and a window the person opened or installed themselves is never involved. `client.js` retries the resize once DSH is up if the browser refused it.
section: Launch mode: app window / normal tab

text: dsh-power-switch README · Launch mode: app window / normal tab：Filling the work area is as far as an automatic action goes: **true fullscreen, taskbar included, needs one gesture**, which the browser will not let a page supply for itself (measured: a load-time `requestFullscreen()` is refused, the same call after a real click reaches 2048x1152, and **F11** does it from the browser). Press `F11` in the app window when you want that; the plugin does not press keys for you.
section: Launch mode: app window / normal tab

text: dsh-power-switch README · Launch mode: app window / normal tab：One press of the card's switch does three things: it saves the setting, updates the desktop shortcut, and restarts DSH. The setting is written to the `dsh-power-switch` section of `$DSH_HOME/settings.yaml` and to the composition entry as well, so the choice survives a restart even when the host serves no settings provider.
section: Launch mode: app window / normal tab

Neither change breaks this plugin:

text: dsh-power-switch README · Desktop shortcut：Switching to the app window adopts the existing DSH shortcut, or creates `DSH 启动器` when none exists; switching back to a normal tab restores the original launch method. The original target, arguments, icon and description are recorded in `shortcut-backup.txt` in the state directory, so the change can be undone at any time.

dsh-power-switch README · Desktop shortcut：What the shortcut points at is **a copy of the launcher in the state directory**, not the packaged one: `shortcut-launch.vbs`, written there on every boot beside that record and beside `restore-shortcut.vbs`. An icon that stops working the moment its plugin is uninstalled is not worth placing, so the file the icon names is one the uninstaller cannot delete. What it does with a double-click:

dsh-power-switch README · Desktop shortcut：1. **The plugin is installed** — a profile under the harness home still **names it in its manifest** (`dsh.profile.bundles` in `<profile>\package.json`, the list the host loads plugins from) *and* carries `<profile>\node_modules\dsh-power-switch\scripts\launch-dsh.vbs`. The copy hands that launcher the arguments it arrived with, waits, and forwards its exit code. The launch path is still `launch-dsh.mjs` through `launch-dsh.vbs`, so a normal start is unchanged; a boot re-points an icon adopted by an earlier version at this copy.
2. **The plugin is gone** — no profile names it any more, so it replays the record through `restore-shortcut.vbs`: the shortcut is the one you had before this plugin ever touched it (or is removed, if this plugin created it), and one dialog says so. The next double-click starts DSH exactly as it used to.

dsh-power-switch README · Desktop shortcut：The manifest is the authority rather than a recorded path **or a surviving directory**, and both halves of that were measured rather than assumed. Uninstalling a `link:` install rewrites the manifest but leaves the junction in `node_modules`; a launcher file that still resolves is therefore not evidence that the plugin is installed, and treating it as evidence is exactly how an icon keeps launching a plugin that is gone while the restore never happens. The recorded path that an earlier build wrote has the same failure mode, which is why a boot deletes it.

dsh-power-switch README · Desktop shortcut：Which harness home the launch means is **answered by looking, not by picking one**: the environment's `DSH_HOME`, the `--home` the shortcut carries and the default `~/.dsh` are each searched for a profile whose manifest names the plugin, and the home that has it wins — and is the one exported to the launcher, so the wrapper reads the state directory belonging to the launcher it was handed. A `DSH_HOME` that changed after the shortcut was created therefore cannot make an installed plugin look uninstalled, and an icon cannot decide to put itself back while the plugin is still there.

dsh-power-switch README · Desktop shortcut：Nothing in this layer is a fixed path. `shortcut-launch.vbs` uses its own folder, the harness home above, DSH's `profiles` directory (the same constant the CLI resolves `--profile` against) and `<profile>\node_modules\<package>` — where pnpm puts a direct dependency, and where DSH says pnpm-managed entries stay authoritative. `restore-shortcut.vbs` uses its own folder, then `%DSH_HOME%`, then `%USERPROFILE%\.dsh`, and the `.lnk` it rewrites is the one named in the record. `make-shortcut.vbs` asks the shell for `Desktop` rather than composing it, which is why a redirected or non-English desktop works, and names `%SystemRoot%\System32\wscript.exe` with a bare-name fallback. Every one of those is derived at run time, so an install under any user name, drive or directory behaves the same.

dsh-power-switch README · Desktop shortcut：Those dialogs are shown **in the language of the Windows the person is using**, because this is a Windows dialog: the scripts read `HKCU\Control Panel\International\LocaleName`, falling back to English, and `DSH_POWER_SWITCH_LANG=zh|en` overrides both. The translations live in `shortcut-messages.txt` in the state directory rather than in the scripts, which cannot carry them: wscript reads a `.vbs` as ANSI, so Chinese written into one arrives as mojibake — and reading the file as UTF-16 instead would make it a binary blob in the repository with no reviewable diff. English is not duplicated into the table; it is the text compiled into each call site and the fallback whenever a key or the whole file is missing.

dsh-power-switch README · Desktop shortcut：Why this layer is necessary: `dsh web` hands its URL to the default browser, so it always opens a tab. It has no app-window option, and that hand-off runs a platform opener with a scrubbed environment, so no plugin can intercept it. The window shape for the next launch can therefore only be chosen by whatever launches dsh — which is this package's launcher, `scripts/launch-dsh.mjs` (wrapped by `launch-dsh.vbs`). It reads the stored mode, starts the host with the recorded launch command when no host is running, waits for the token the host prints, and opens the window in that mode.

dsh-power-switch README · Desktop shortcut："Recorded launch command" means the plugin writes its own launch facts (`process.execPath`, argv, cwd) to `boot.json` in the state directory while it runs, and the launcher replays them verbatim. The earlier implementation rebuilt `<checkout>/apps/cli/lib/bin.js`, a path that exists only in a DSH source checkout and therefore failed under every other installation.

dsh-power-switch README · Desktop shortcut：Two facts a cold start cannot guess are **derived or recorded, never assumed**. The port is read back from what the host wrote about itself: the authenticated URL of its last run, then a `--port` in the recorded command line, then the documented default; and the wait for the host's readiness line accepts any loopback port, so a DSH that serves on a non-default port is started and opened rather than waited on for two minutes at a port it never used. The harness home is written into the shortcut as `--home <dir>` and handed down as `DSH_HOME` (a variable that is already set wins), so a shortcut double-clicked from Explorer reads the same state directory as the host even when the person's own shell is the only place `DSH_HOME` was ever defined.

dsh-power-switch README · Desktop shortcut：A launch that fails says so. The wrapper waits for the launcher, and a non-zero exit opens a message box with the exit code, the last lines of the log and the log path — a shortcut is double-clicked, and a wrapper that exits silently is indistinguishable from a shortcut that was never wired up.

The launcher can also be run directly:

dsh-power-switch README · Desktop shortcut：```powershell
node scripts/launch-dsh.mjs                            # the mode from the setting
node scripts/launch-dsh.mjs --app                      # force an app window for this run
node scripts/launch-dsh.mjs --tab                      # force a normal tab for this run
node scripts/launch-dsh.mjs --cli <path to the dsh CLI entry>   # name the CLI entry

dsh-power-switch README · Desktop shortcut：The launcher never starts a duplicate instance: when a host is already serving it only opens the window, and when the port answers but no live token can be obtained it refuses to start and reports why.

dsh-power-switch README · The desktop app：DSH's desktop build (`DeepSeek Harness.exe`, packaged with Electron) runs under `--profile desktop`, which is a separate install from this plugin's `web` profile. The plugin **can** be installed into the desktop profile, and since 1.1.8 shutdown and since 1.1.9 restart both actually work there — over different channels than on the command line.

dsh-power-switch README · The desktop app：**Why the channel has to differ.** The desktop host is a child the Electron main process `fork`s. Its `ctx.appExit` is DSH's own `shutdown(code)`, and in `@deepseek-ai/dsh` 0.2.x that is:

```js
shutdown(code){ return start(code, false) }   // forceAfterDispose = false
// → completeOnce(code), i.e. process.exitCode = code
```

dsh-power-switch README · The desktop app：It sets an exit code and **never calls `process.exit`**; only a disposal that overruns 5 s is forced. A CLI host still goes away because the CLI's own main finishes. An Electron main process keeps its event loop alive, so setting a code closes nothing. The observable result: the route answers ok, the page says "closing", and DSH is still running.

dsh-power-switch README · The desktop app：The desktop app's own stop channel is IPC. The Electron main process sends `{ type: 'shutdown' }`; `dsh-desktop-host` answers by running `await shutdown.shutdown(0)`, reporting `{ type: 'shutdown-complete' }` and then `process.disconnect()`. 1.1.6 asked that way **first** (removed in 1.1.9, for the reason below): `isDesktopHost()` decides on "has `process.send` and `connected === true`", and `requestDesktopShutdown()` sends exactly that message. Only when the channel is unusable does it fall back to `appExit` and then `SIGTERM`.

dsh-power-switch README · The desktop app：The check is the IPC channel rather than the executable name on purpose: a source checkout, a packaged install and a custom installer all produce different executable names, while the channel is the fact that matters — a CLI host does not have one.

dsh-power-switch README · The desktop app：**The IPC channel is not enough, and that is what 1.1.8 fixes.** `{ type: 'shutdown' }` still lands on that same `shutdown()` — set the code, clear its own watchdog, stay alive. Measured on the packaged 0.2.0-rc.2: the route answered ok, the page said "closing", DSH kept running. So the desktop case needs a terminator outside the DSH tree. What the plugin does now:

dsh-power-switch README · The desktop app：1.1.8 also sent the IPC `{ type: 'shutdown' }` before terminating. **That step was removed in 1.1.9**: the main process stops the host as soon as it receives it, so the host often died before the helper had started. The main process then read the child's exit as a failure and showed the crash dialog while the window stayed up — which looked, in the log, like nothing at all after `desktop host:`. Sending the IPC first bought a delay, not a clean exit.

dsh-power-switch README · The desktop app：| Approach | Result |
|---|---|
| Python `TerminateProcess` on the main pid | ✅ works, no leftovers |
| PowerShell `Process.Kill()` on the main pid | ✅ works, no leftovers |
| VBScript `Win32_Process.Terminate` via WMI on the main pid | ✅ works, gone within 100 ms — this is what the helper uses now |
| `taskkill /PID <main> /F` | ❌ `ERROR: Access denied` |
| Killing every child instead | ⚠️ the whole app does exit, but the main process shows a crash dialog first |
| Asking the main process over IPC | ❌ there is no quit channel (none of its 19 channels offers quit or restart) |

dsh-power-switch README · The desktop app：`taskkill` being refused is not a sandbox artefact: the packaged app installs a `dshMandatoryUpdatePolicy` restricting what helper processes may do to it, and a real `TerminateProcess` handle is not covered by it — which is the path PowerShell's `Process.Kill()` takes.

dsh-power-switch README · The desktop app：**Why the helper is VBScript and not PowerShell — this is what 1.1.9 fixes.** A process created by WMI gets a **new console**. `powershell.exe` is a CONSOLE-subsystem program, so a restart flashed a black command window and put an entry in the taskbar; `-WindowStyle Hidden` only hides a window that already exists, and the frame before it is hidden is still visible. `wscript.exe` is a **GUI-subsystem** program: it never creates a console, so there is nothing to flash and nothing to hide, and the helper's work — wait, check a pid, terminate it, start again — needs no console at all.

dsh-power-switch README · The desktop app：| Step | Why it has to be in that position |
|---|---|
| 1. Kill the main process | The window disappears here |
| 2. Kill the host | The host is the main process's `fork` child; when the parent dies it survives as an orphan holding the port, and the new instance would collide with it |
| 3. Wait | Electron releases its single-instance lock only on exit; starting too early is silently treated as "already running" and discarded |
| 4. Start the executable | Same file, same working directory |

dsh-power-switch README · The desktop app：Steps 2 and 3 are **polls**, not fixed sleeps: whether a process has exited is a fact that can be checked. The first version slept 1200 ms and then 2500 ms, making every restart about 4.5 s; it now usually completes in about a second.

Step 4 is guarded: the executable must still be on disk, and otherwise the app is left closed rather than half-started — which is reported plainly, because a restart that cannot start is a shutdown.

dsh-power-switch README · The desktop app：**Since 1.1.10 the helper does not treat "the call returned" as "it started".** `Shell.Run` hands back no handle, so when 1.1.9 wrote `helper: started` it only knew that nothing had thrown. It now counts processes by name 1.5 s after launching: one is success, none means try once more, and two failures write `the executable did not stay up`. The other way round, if the main process or the host is still alive after both termination attempts, the helper **does not start a second instance** and says why — such an instance loses the single-instance race and exits within a second, which is exactly what "the restart did nothing" looks like from outside.

text: dsh-power-switch README · Desktop shortcut：Switching to the app window adopts the existing DSH shortcut, or creates `DSH 启动器` when none exists; switching back to a normal tab restores the original launch method. The original target, arguments, icon and description are recorded in `shortcut-backup.txt` in the state directory, so the change can be undone at any time.

dsh-power-switch README · Desktop shortcut：What the shortcut points at is **a copy of the launcher in the state directory**, not the packaged one: `shortcut-launch.vbs`, written there on every boot beside that record and beside `restore-shortcut.vbs`. An icon that stops working the moment its plugin is uninstalled is not worth placing, so the file the icon names is one the uninstaller cannot delete. What it does with a double-click:

dsh-power-switch README · Desktop shortcut：1. **The plugin is installed** — a profile under the harness home still **names it in its manifest** (`dsh.profile.bundles` in `<profile>\package.json`, the list the host loads plugins from) *and* carries `<profile>\node_modules\dsh-power-switch\scripts\launch-dsh.vbs`. The copy hands that launcher the arguments it arrived with, waits, and forwards its exit code. The launch path is still `launch-dsh.mjs` through `launch-dsh.vbs`, so a normal start is unchanged; a boot re-points an icon adopted by an earlier version at this copy.
2. **The plugin is gone** — no profile names it any more, so it replays the record through `restore-shortcut.vbs`: the shortcut is the one you had before this plugin ever touched it (or is removed, if this plugin created it), and one dialog says so. The next double-click starts DSH exactly as it used to.

dsh-power-switch README · Desktop shortcut：The manifest is the authority rather than a recorded path **or a surviving directory**, and both halves of that were measured rather than assumed. Uninstalling a `link:` install rewrites the manifest but leaves the junction in `node_modules`; a launcher file that still resolves is therefore not evidence that the plugin is installed, and treating it as evidence is exactly how an icon keeps launching a plugin that is gone while the restore never happens. The recorded path that an earlier build wrote has the same failure mode, which is why a boot deletes it.

dsh-power-switch README · Desktop shortcut：Which harness home the launch means is **answered by looking, not by picking one**: the environment's `DSH_HOME`, the `--home` the shortcut carries and the default `~/.dsh` are each searched for a profile whose manifest names the plugin, and the home that has it wins — and is the one exported to the launcher, so the wrapper reads the state directory belonging to the launcher it was handed. A `DSH_HOME` that changed after the shortcut was created therefore cannot make an installed plugin look uninstalled, and an icon cannot decide to put itself back while the plugin is still there.

dsh-power-switch README · Desktop shortcut：Nothing in this layer is a fixed path. `shortcut-launch.vbs` uses its own folder, the harness home above, DSH's `profiles` directory (the same constant the CLI resolves `--profile` against) and `<profile>\node_modules\<package>` — where pnpm puts a direct dependency, and where DSH says pnpm-managed entries stay authoritative. `restore-shortcut.vbs` uses its own folder, then `%DSH_HOME%`, then `%USERPROFILE%\.dsh`, and the `.lnk` it rewrites is the one named in the record. `make-shortcut.vbs` asks the shell for `Desktop` rather than composing it, which is why a redirected or non-English desktop works, and names `%SystemRoot%\System32\wscript.exe` with a bare-name fallback. Every one of those is derived at run time, so an install under any user name, drive or directory behaves the same.

dsh-power-switch README · Desktop shortcut：Those dialogs are shown **in the language of the Windows the person is using**, because this is a Windows dialog: the scripts read `HKCU\Control Panel\International\LocaleName`, falling back to English, and `DSH_POWER_SWITCH_LANG=zh|en` overrides both. The translations live in `shortcut-messages.txt` in the state directory rather than in the scripts, which cannot carry them: wscript reads a `.vbs` as ANSI, so Chinese written into one arrives as mojibake — and reading the file as UTF-16 instead would make it a binary blob in the repository with no reviewable diff. English is not duplicated into the table; it is the text compiled into each call site and the fallback whenever a key or the whole file is missing.

dsh-power-switch README · Desktop shortcut：Why this layer is necessary: `dsh web` hands its URL to the default browser, so it always opens a tab. It has no app-window option, and that hand-off runs a platform opener with a scrubbed environment, so no plugin can intercept it. The window shape for the next launch can therefore only be chosen by whatever launches dsh — which is this package's launcher, `scripts/launch-dsh.mjs` (wrapped by `launch-dsh.vbs`). It reads the stored mode, starts the host with the recorded launch command when no host is running, waits for the token the host prints, and opens the window in that mode.

dsh-power-switch README · Desktop shortcut："Recorded launch command" means the plugin writes its own launch facts (`process.execPath`, argv, cwd) to `boot.json` in the state directory while it runs, and the launcher replays them verbatim. The earlier implementation rebuilt `<checkout>/apps/cli/lib/bin.js`, a path that exists only in a DSH source checkout and therefore failed under every other installation.

dsh-power-switch README · Desktop shortcut：Two facts a cold start cannot guess are **derived or recorded, never assumed**. The port is read back from what the host wrote about itself: the authenticated URL of its last run, then a `--port` in the recorded command line, then the documented default; and the wait for the host's readiness line accepts any loopback port, so a DSH that serves on a non-default port is started and opened rather than waited on for two minutes at a port it never used. The harness home is written into the shortcut as `--home <dir>` and handed down as `DSH_HOME` (a variable that is already set wins), so a shortcut double-clicked from Explorer reads the same state directory as the host even when the person's own shell is the only place `DSH_HOME` was ever defined.

dsh-power-switch README · Desktop shortcut：A launch that fails says so. The wrapper waits for the launcher, and a non-zero exit opens a message box with the exit code, the last lines of the log and the log path — a shortcut is double-clicked, and a wrapper that exits silently is indistinguishable from a shortcut that was never wired up.

The launcher can also be run directly:

dsh-power-switch README · Desktop shortcut：```powershell

node scripts/launch-dsh.mjs --app                      # force an app window for this run
node scripts/launch-dsh.mjs --tab                      # force a normal tab for this run
node scripts/launch-dsh.mjs --cli <path to the dsh CLI entry>   # name the CLI entry

dsh-power-switch README · Desktop shortcut：The launcher never starts a duplicate instance: when a host is already serving it only opens the window, and when the port answers but no live token can be obtained it refuses to start and reports why.

dsh-power-switch README · The desktop app：DSH's desktop build (`DeepSeek Harness.exe`, packaged with Electron) runs under `--profile desktop`, which is a separate install from this plugin's `web` profile. The plugin **can** be installed into the desktop profile, and since 1.1.8 shutdown and since 1.1.9 restart both actually work there — over different channels than on the command line.

dsh-power-switch README · The desktop app：**Why the channel has to differ.** The desktop host is a child the Electron main process `fork`s. Its `ctx.appExit` is DSH's own `shutdown(code)`, and in `@deepseek-ai/dsh` 0.2.x that is:

```js
shutdown(code){ return start(code, false) }   // forceAfterDispose = false
// → completeOnce(code), i.e. process.exitCode = code
```

dsh-power-switch README · The desktop app：It sets an exit code and **never calls `process.exit`**; only a disposal that overruns 5 s is forced. A CLI host still goes away because the CLI's own main finishes. An Electron main process keeps its event loop alive, so setting a code closes nothing. The observable result: the route answers ok, the page says "closing", and DSH is still running.

dsh-power-switch README · The desktop app：The desktop app's own stop channel is IPC. The Electron main process sends `{ type: 'shutdown' }`; `dsh-desktop-host` answers by running `await shutdown.shutdown(0)`, reporting `{ type: 'shutdown-complete' }` and then `process.disconnect()`. 1.1.6 asked that way **first** (removed in 1.1.9, for the reason below): `isDesktopHost()` decides on "has `process.send` and `connected === true`", and `requestDesktopShutdown()` sends exactly that message. Only when the channel is unusable does it fall back to `appExit` and then `SIGTERM`.

dsh-power-switch README · The desktop app：The check is the IPC channel rather than the executable name on purpose: a source checkout, a packaged install and a custom installer all produce different executable names, while the channel is the fact that matters — a CLI host does not have one.

dsh-power-switch README · The desktop app：**The IPC channel is not enough, and that is what 1.1.8 fixes.** `{ type: 'shutdown' }` still lands on that same `shutdown()` — set the code, clear its own watchdog, stay alive. Measured on the packaged 0.2.0-rc.2: the route answered ok, the page said "closing", DSH kept running. So the desktop case needs a terminator outside the DSH tree. What the plugin does now:

dsh-power-switch README · The desktop app：1.1.8 also sent the IPC `{ type: 'shutdown' }` before terminating. **That step was removed in 1.1.9**: the main process stops the host as soon as it receives it, so the host often died before the helper had started. The main process then read the child's exit as a failure and showed the crash dialog while the window stayed up — which looked, in the log, like nothing at all after `desktop host:`. Sending the IPC first bought a delay, not a clean exit.

dsh-power-switch README · The desktop app：| Approach | Result |
|---|---|
| Python `TerminateProcess` on the main pid | ✅ works, no leftovers |
| PowerShell `Process.Kill()` on the main pid | ✅ works, no leftovers |
| VBScript `Win32_Process.Terminate` via WMI on the main pid | ✅ works, gone within 100 ms — this is what the helper uses now |
| `taskkill /PID <main> /F` | ❌ `ERROR: Access denied` |
| Killing every child instead | ⚠️ the whole app does exit, but the main process shows a crash dialog first |
| Asking the main process over IPC | ❌ there is no quit channel (none of its 19 channels offers quit or restart) |

dsh-power-switch README · The desktop app：`taskkill` being refused is not a sandbox artefact: the packaged app installs a `dshMandatoryUpdatePolicy` restricting what helper processes may do to it, and a real `TerminateProcess` handle is not covered by it — which is the path PowerShell's `Process.Kill()` takes.

dsh-power-switch README · The desktop app：**Why the helper is VBScript and not PowerShell — this is what 1.1.9 fixes.** A process created by WMI gets a **new console**. `powershell.exe` is a CONSOLE-subsystem program, so a restart flashed a black command window and put an entry in the taskbar; `-WindowStyle Hidden` only hides a window that already exists, and the frame before it is hidden is still visible. `wscript.exe` is a **GUI-subsystem** program: it never creates a console, so there is nothing to flash and nothing to hide, and the helper's work — wait, check a pid, terminate it, start again — needs no console at all.

dsh-power-switch README · The desktop app：`CREATE_NO_WINDOW` was tried too (`Win32_ProcessStartup.CreateFlags = 0x08000000`, the only guarantee that no console is created at all). All three spellings answered `ReturnValue=21` on this machine — the parameter is refused — so the route went around it.

dsh-power-switch README · The desktop app：One related failure is easy to miss: the helper first started DSH with `Start-Process`, so the new instance **inherited the helper's console**. Closing that black window sends `CTRL_CLOSE_EVENT` to everything attached to it, and the freshly started DSH exited with it. DSH is now started by the helper through WMI as well: it inherits no console and belongs to no job object, so closing some other window cannot take it down.

dsh-power-switch README · The desktop app：**Restart, since 1.1.9.** It reuses that same terminator: rather than replaying a command line, it walks a fixed four-step order and finally starts the executable again.

dsh-power-switch README · The desktop app：| Step | Why it has to be in that position |
|---|---|
| 1. Kill the main process | The window disappears here |
| 2. Kill the host | The host is the main process's `fork` child; when the parent dies it survives as an orphan holding the port, and the new instance would collide with it |
| 3. Wait | Electron releases its single-instance lock only on exit; starting too early is silently treated as "already running" and discarded |
| 4. Start the executable | Same file, same working directory |

dsh-power-switch README · The desktop app：Steps 2 and 3 are **polls**, not fixed sleeps: whether a process has exited is a fact that can be checked. The first version slept 1200 ms and then 2500 ms, making every restart about 4.5 s; it now usually completes in about a second.

Step 4 is guarded: the executable must still be on disk, and otherwise the app is left closed rather than half-started — which is reported plainly, because a restart that cannot start is a shutdown.

dsh-power-switch README · The desktop app：**Since 1.1.10 the helper does not treat "the call returned" as "it started".** `Shell.Run` hands back no handle, so when 1.1.9 wrote `helper: started` it only knew that nothing had thrown. It now counts processes by name 1.5 s after launching: one is success, none means try once more, and two failures write `the executable did not stay up`. The other way round, if the main process or the host is still alive after both termination attempts, the helper **does not start a second instance** and says why — such an instance loses the single-instance race and exits within a second, which is exactly what "the restart did nothing" looks like from outside.

dsh-power-switch README · The desktop app：That version also fixes two things that go wrong on other machines: the working directory is now set before launching (`WScript.Shell` uses the script's own, and a WMI-created helper sits in System32 — this was missed in 1.1.9), and `wscript.exe` is resolved through `%SystemRoot%` instead of PATH.

dsh-power-switch README · The desktop app：**Why restart does not replay the launch command line.** It used to, and the desktop app's argv is `app.asar\dsh <profile> <runtime> ...` — a child process's command line. Replaying it only produces an orphan host with no Electron shell, and no window ever appears. So `looksLikeDshWeb()` judging the desktop case un-replayable is correct; what changed in 1.1.9 is that there is a way to restart **without** replaying, not that the judgement was loosened.

dsh-power-switch README · The desktop app：**And one step has to stay asynchronous.** If `gracefulExit` resolves at once, the watchdog reads that as "the handover finished" and stands down (`graceful exit settled; the watchdog stands down`), leaving the process in place — which is precisely how this route used to report success and close nothing. So the desktop branch's promise does not resolve until the process is really gone, and the watchdog's forced exit stays armed. The "could not kill it" case follows the same rule: it stays pending and lets the watchdog escalate.

| Restart | **Works** since 1.1.9: the same helper kills the main process, kills the host, waits for the single-instance lock to be released, and starts the executable again. It no longer replays the command line, and no longer answers `unsupported-host` |

dsh-power-switch README · State and logs：State is kept outside the package for two reasons: the package may sit in a read-only store, and the log contains authenticated token URLs and local paths, so a log inside the package would be a log inside the repository.

dsh-power-switch README · Configuration：| Key | Default | Meaning |
|---|---|---|
| `launchMode` | `tab` | Window for the next launch: `tab` or `app` |
| `delayMs` | `1000` | Milliseconds to wait after answering before the exit begins. The answer itself needs 1200 ms to reach the browser, so that is the floor: `0` means "as soon as the answer is out", and anything below 1200 waits 1200 |
| `exitCode` | `0` | The status the DSH process ends with, for whatever started it — a shell (`$LASTEXITCODE`), a service manager, a script. `0` is success, so a non-zero value is for a wrapper that wants to tell "the person closed DSH" apart from a crash |

dsh-power-switch README · Configuration：All four are for a DSH **started from a local build**: the `dsh web` command line, a source checkout, or something a script or service manager pulls up. The desktop app (Electron) manages its own exit, its launch-mode switch is refused outright (see "The desktop app" above), and nothing reads `delayMs` or `exitCode` there; only `hard` still means something, being the forced-exit path.
`launchMode` is switched from the card. The other three are edited from the card's own **Advanced settings** block, which writes them to `settings.json` in the state directory. On a host that still has the registered-namespace settings API, the same save is written to the settings document as well, so the two surfaces cannot disagree; the recorded value is the one that governs, and deleting `settings.json` hands the decision back to the loader row's `config:` and the settings document.
dsh-power-switch README · Configuration：The card opens on the two power controls alone. The launch-mode switch and the three advanced values share one **Advanced settings** fold that starts closed.

dsh-power-switch README · Configuration：The card sends **no** delay of its own: `delayMs` governs every exit, the card's buttons included. dsh-power-switch README · Security boundary：All six routes (`GET /config`, `GET /app-window`, `POST /shutdown`, `POST /restart`, `POST /shortcut`, `POST /settings`) share one floor: loopback requests only. The peer must be `127.0.0.1`/`::1`, and any forwarding header (`forwarded`, `x-forwarded-for`, `x-real-ip`, `x-forwarded-host`) is refused.

dsh-power-switch README · Security boundary：The write routes (`shutdown`/`restart`/`shortcut`/`settings`) additionally require `Origin` to match `Host` exactly. The read routes (`GET /config`, `GET /app-window`) accept a missing `Origin`, because some hosts issue their own requests without it, while still requiring loopback and still refusing forwarding headers; that difference is documented in the code.

dsh-power-switch README · Security boundary：`POST /shortcut` is the only route that produces a file outside the package, so its body accepts exactly one fixed action (`scan` / `install` / `restore`); the directory, file name, target and arguments are all derived by the host from its own installation location, and the client cannot choose any of them.

The plugin reads no credentials, makes no network requests and never touches session content.

Two boundaries are worth stating plainly rather than leaving to be discovered:

dsh-power-switch README · Security boundary：- **`boot.json` is a trust boundary.** The restart replays the command line the running host recorded for itself, verbatim — that is the whole design, and it is why no installation path is ever reconstructed. Anyone who can write the state directory can therefore have that command executed with your privileges. That is not a privilege escalation (the same is true of `settings.yaml`, the profile's plugin list, and every other file the harness reads), and it is exactly why the state directory lives inside your user profile and never inside the package. Treat write access to `$DSH_HOME` as equivalent to running code as yourself. Two more files sit on the same boundary. `shortcut-launch.vbs` and `restore-shortcut.vbs` are refreshed from the package at every boot and are meant to be run — the desktop shortcut itself starts the first one — so a state-directory writer could put something else under those names; the launch copy only ever starts the launcher a profile resolves to, and the repair copy only ever edits a `.lnk` from the recorded fields, but treat both like any other executable in your profile.
